name: Allen Ginsberg
summary: Ginsberg opposed the Vietnam War and nuclear arms production, and practiced nonviolent direct action. He challenged censorship of sexual expression, opposed sodomy laws, and advocated legal cannabis sales and medical care for opioid addiction.

notes: Reviewed the full statement bank, including candidates, against Collected Poems 1947–1997, Deliberate Prose, interviews, and records of court and protest activity. Searched economy (taxation, public spending, banking, industrial policy and welfare), government (elections, representation, executive authority, courts and the draft), world and globalism (Vietnam, Nicaragua, Tibet, Israel and Palestine, alliances, aid and international institutions), liberty (drug laws, censorship, surveillance and police accountability), society and culture (race, historical redress, sexuality, marriage, and religion in government and education), ecology and technology (industrial growth, energy, nuclear waste and climate), and means (civil disobedience, revolution, and political violence). Follow-up searches on the widest lines covered racial exclusion, territorial and minority autonomy, secular government, monarchy and republicanism, trade and supranational institutions, and class struggle and labor unions. Checked the local Gutenberg catalog, maintainer library, Miller Center index, and MediaSum. Ginsberg expressly supported legal cannabis sales, while distinguishing them from medical treatment for opioid addiction and possible licensing for psychedelics. His advocacy of a national apology for slavery settles the apology item, while the sources reviewed give no specific policy for repairing the material harm of slavery. In the 1969 Fifth Estate interview he declined to give a categorical answer on the admissibility of political violence.
